maṅgala
(‘the auspicious’)
------------------------------------------
See AṢṬAMAṄGALAS.
The planet mars, one of the nine mentioned in the works on अस्त्रोलोग्य् is also known as मङ्गल. Its other names are: अङ्गारक, कुज, Bhauma, Āvaneya, Lohitāṅga and Krūrākṣa. It is supposed to rule over the colour red and ruled over by God कार्त्तिकेय or सुब्रह्मण्य and the element of fire. It is said to be a malefic planet but give beneficial results in southern direction. Its nature is that of a क्षत्त्रिय. Its residence in the body is the marrow whereas outside, it lives in the fire-place.
Actually, these details are useful in astrological predictions.

maṅgalasūtra
(‘the auspicious thread’)
------------------------------------------
Vivāha or मर्रिअगे is considered as an important saṁskāra or sacrament in the life of every Hindu. One of the primary steps in this sacrament is the tying of the मङ्गलसूत्र by the bridegroom round the neck of the bride, which she is expected to wear as long as her husband is alive. This rite comes after the सप्तपदी. (See SAPTAPADĪ.) The sūtra generally consists of a string with golden and other beads including a coin-shaped amulet.
Though this is considered as one of the most important aspects of the मर्रिअगे ritual now, it has not been mentioned in the earlier dharmaśāstra works. The Śaunakasmṛti is the earliest treatise that mentions it. The practice must have come into vogue around A.

.
In some works, the tying of कङ्कण (protective cord) by the couple to each other’s hands is mentioned as ‘kaṅkaṇabandhana’. This cord itself is called मङ्गलसूत्र.

maṅkigītā
(‘song of [the sage] Maṅki’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā (‘Song of God’) by its extraordinary beauty, elegance and spiritual eminence, inspired the emergence of many other gītās, most of them being in the Mahābhārata itself. One such is this Maṅkigītā. It is a part of the Śāntiparva (ch. 177, verses 5 to 54).
The sage Maṅki purchased two oxen, yoked them and was taking them to a field. It so happened that a camel lying on the road, suddenly got up when the oxen had just approached it and started running with the yoke on its neck and the two bullocks hanging! Having lost his source of livelihood, Maṅki developed वैराग्य or dispassion and taught this गीता to his own मिन्द्.
The gist of the Maṅkigītā can be given as follows:
The मिन्द् is full of desires. These desires can never be satiated. A person takes a lot of trouble in acquiring wealth. But the accumulated wealth tempts thieves and robbers who take it away, harming or even killing its owner. Loss of wealth also generates intense suffering.
Hence one must destroy the seven enemies—kāma (lust), krodha (anger), लोभ (greed), मोह (delusion), मद (intoxication), mātsarya (jealousy) and अहङ्कार (egoism).
The best way to conquer desires is to stop सङ्कल्प (deciding to work for fulfilling the desire).
By attaining योग (concentration of मिन्द् on ब्रह्मन्) I will become happy. Then you (= the मिन्द्) can never dupe me into sorrow and suffering!
See also BHAGAVADGĪTĀ.
